name: Chloe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Brightwell Medical Supply, a small wholesaler that stocks independent pharmacies with things like cold remedies, bandages and baby formula. I start with the AI assistant I've set up, which reads the overnight sales from forty pharmacies and flags what's running low. Then I spend the day on what it can't do: chasing a dressing maker whose factory flooded, or deciding whether to gamble on extra flu stock.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay, and the town. I'm good at this and I know it, but Brightwell pays well under the big wholesalers, and there are maybe two jobs like mine within reach. I share a flat with my friend Nadia, and I've still got a master's loan, so there's less than a month of money in my account most of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I've had fun with these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they were sold as magic, and the people who believed the sales pitch should be embarrassed. Online I'd write a little thread about what actually works in buying, with examples. I'd be the nerd who says it's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and my skills with the tools are a small edge, not a huge one. It doesn't fix my pay, my loan or the lack of other jobs here. I'd still be stuck at Brightwell on a wage that doesn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small automations, like the low-stock alerts, and use them to ask for a raise at my review in March. I'd join the pharmacy workers' union, which lets wholesale staff in, because pay is the real problem in this picture. And I'd set up a standing transfer of eighty a month to savings, even if it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, I think. Safe, but stuck. The same worry about money, just without anything exciting to balance it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said stuck. What would unstick you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A city job, but that means rent I can't afford on what I'd save. Or Brightwell paying me what I'm worth, which the owner says isn't possible because margins are thin. Both feel far away in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your tools are only a small edge, would you stop using them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No way. The AI tools save me two hours a day, and I spend those hours on supplier calls, which is where good buying really happens. I'd just stop pretending they'll change the world.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful**, but they were **sold as magic**.
I'd post examples of what **actually works** in buying.
think: My job's safe, and my AI skills are a **small edge**, not a big one.
I'd still be **stuck at Brightwell** on a wage that doesn't move.
do: Build more **low-stock alerts** and use them to argue for a raise in March.
Join the **pharmacy workers' union**, which accepts wholesale staff.
Set a **standing transfer** of eighty a month into savings.
feel: **Flat**: safe but stuck, with the same money worries.
S0.quote: The AI tools save me two hours a day, and I spend those hours on supplier calls, which is where good buying really happens.
fieldNote: She's a **daily AI user** who sees the tools as time-savers, not magic.
Her real problem in this picture is **low pay** and few local jobs, so she turns to the union.
She's mildly **disappointed** that the plateau removes the excitement.

steps.text: Build more low-stock alerts to support a March raise request
Join the pharmacy workers' union as a wholesale member
Set a standing eighty-a-month transfer into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying, planning, checking. That's my whole job description, read out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, not just kept by owners. If one buyer with AI does the work of three, then the other two deserve retraining on full pay. I'd say that at work and online. I'd also say buyers who know the tools should help design the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd survive, because I'm already the person who builds the systems. But Brightwell has three buyers, and I don't see three by 2029. My friend Owen on the team doesn't touch the tools, and I'd lie awake about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead the rollout before someone from outside does it, and write a plan that moves Owen and the junior buyer into supplier quality checks. I'd take an online course in pharmacy supply regulation, which is a field where a human still signs things off. And I'd quietly apply for two or three roles in the city, just to know my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and sick at the same time. I'd love the work, but I'd hate being the face of a change that cost my friends their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lead the rollout. What if the owner takes your plan and cuts Owen anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the union and make a fuss, properly. I wouldn't let my work be used as a cover for sacking him. I'd probably start looking harder for the exit as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your pay is low. Would leading the rollout change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, and I'd ask for it in writing first. I'm not doing a manager's job on a buyer's wage. But I know the owner, and I'd probably get a small bump and a lot of thank-yous.

say: I'd say AI **gains must be shared**, with retraining on full pay.
I'd say buyers who **know the tools** should help design the change.
think: I'd probably **survive**, because I already build the systems.
Brightwell won't keep **three buyers**, and my friend Owen would be at risk.
do: Offer to **lead the rollout** with a plan moving colleagues into quality checks.
Take an online course in **pharmacy supply regulation**.
Apply quietly for **two or three** city roles.
feel: **Excited and sick** at once about being the face of the change.
S1.quote: I'd love the work, but I'd hate being the face of a change that cost my friends their jobs.
fieldNote: She is **ahead of the curve** and wants to shape the rollout rather than suffer it.
Her **loyalty to colleagues** shapes her plan: she'd fight to move Owen, not drop him.
Her own income isn't secure on **low pay** and thin savings, so she keeps a city exit open.

steps.text: Lead Brightwell's AI ordering rollout with a plan for colleagues
Take an online course in pharmacy supply regulation
Apply quietly for two or three buyer roles in the city
Take any unfair cuts to the pharmacy workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even I'd struggle to keep up with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs a public response, fast: income support, free retraining, and a share of the profits going back to people. I'd be organising, not just posting. I'd want buyers and warehouse staff in the same room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my clever setups are worthless by 2028, because AGI does everything I do and better. The warehouse might last until robots arrive around 2031, but I'm not a warehouse person, and I've got no savings to ride out a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd go all in on whatever new work appears around these systems: checking the AI's buying, handling supplier disputes, regulatory sign-offs. I'd take any short course that gets me there in months, not years. And I'd move back in with my mum for a year to wipe out my rent, even though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the one who sees change coming and enjoys it, but AGI by 2028 is too fast and I've got nothing to land on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd organise. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a group with buyers from the other wholesalers nearby, maybe twenty of us, and push the union to bargain as a block. Alone we're nothing, but together we could at least get notice and payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back with your mum. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grim but survivable. She'd be glad to have me and ask a hundred questions a day. It would be a step backwards at twenty-seven, but it buys me a year.

say: I'd call for **income support**, free retraining and a share of profits.
I'd **organise** buyers and warehouse staff together, not just post online.
think: With **no savings**, I can't ride out a gap until something new appears.
do: Chase new work **checking AI buying** and handling supplier disputes.
Take **short courses** lasting months, not years.
Move back in with her **mum** for a year to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed**: too fast, with nothing to **land on**.
S2.quote: I'm usually the one who sees change coming and enjoys it, but AGI by 2028 is too fast and I've got nothing to land on.
fieldNote: Even an **early adopter** feels overrun by a two-year timeline.
She turns to **organising** across firms, not just within Brightwell.
Living with her **mum** is her money buffer, since savings are near zero.

steps.text: Apply for roles checking AI buying and supplier disputes
Take short courses that finish within months
Move back in with her mum for a year
Set up a bargaining group with buyers from nearby wholesalers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something. I'd use every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build proper transition plans, so let's make governments do it. At work I'd be the person running workshops on what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel more in control. Five years is enough to become the person who checks and signs off what the AI buys, at least for a while. After 2031, though, even that might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd finish the pharmacy supply regulation course and apply for quality roles at bigger wholesalers. I'd lead Brightwell's switch to AI buying to get the experience on my CV. And I'd save hard, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, so I have two months behind me by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the busy kind. I'd be making lists and ticking things off, which is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even quality roles might shrink after 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't plan yet. Maybe there's a role in regulation, writing the rules for these systems, where people want a human with buying experience. I'd keep my eyes open rather than pretend I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for one of those jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it paid enough to cover city rent. I'd miss Nadia and the flat. There's no future for me in this town if my firm shrinks to one person and a machine.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **proper transition plans**, so governments must act.
I'd run **workshops** at work about what's coming.
think: I'd feel more **in control**, with time to become the AI checker.
do: Finish the **regulation course** and apply for quality roles at bigger wholesalers.
Lead Brightwell's switch to **AI buying** for CV experience.
Save **150 a month** to reach two months' cushion by 2029.
S3.quote: There's no future for me in this town if my firm shrinks to one person and a machine.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a sense of **control** that two years doesn't.
She's **honest about limits**: she can't plan past 2031 and says so.
She'd **leave town** for a quality or regulation job if pay covered city rent.

steps.text: Finish the pharmacy supply regulation course in year one
Lead Brightwell's switch to AI buying
Save 150 a month toward two months' cushion
Move to the city for a quality role at a bigger wholesaler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it for proper public retraining and a fair share of the gains. I'd keep pushing that at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd have time to move from buying into regulation or quality, build some savings, maybe even get ahead of it. The robot part, around 2039, matters less to me, because I'm not a hands-on worker anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year doing the regulation course and the second applying for a quality role in the city. I'd keep using AI daily, so I understand it better than the people who'll be managing it. And I'd pay off the master's loan by 2030, so I'm not carrying debt into the big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small worry I'm being too confident. Ten years can go fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be too confident. What would knock that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If regulation goes to AI as well, which it might, my plan falls apart. I'd be relying on governments wanting a human name on the paperwork. That's a bet, not a certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, and people like my mum, who'd be sixty by then and working in a shop. The ten years helps me, but it doesn't help everyone the same way.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift for public retraining and shared gains.
I'd keep pushing that at the **union** and online.
think: I'd be **fine**, with time to move into regulation or quality.
The **2039 robots** matter less to me, because my work isn't hands-on.
do: Take the **regulation course** in year one and apply for city quality roles in year two.
Keep using **AI daily** to understand it better than managers.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a small worry she's **too confident**.
S4.quote: I'd be relying on governments wanting a human name on the paperwork. That's a bet, not a certainty.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **plan a whole path**: course, move, debt cleared.
She's **self-aware** about the bet she's making on regulation needing a human.
She worries about **others**, like Owen and her mum, more than herself here.

steps.text: Take the pharmacy regulation course in the first year
Apply for quality roles at city wholesalers in year two
Keep using AI daily in Brightwell's buying
Pay off her master's loan by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone like me who loves this stuff would have nothing to land on. What would help is a public income for the gap, and short, free courses that lead straight into the new jobs, not three-year degrees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pharmacies. If buying goes fully automated, the small independent pharmacies lose the person who'd ring around to find them baby formula in a shortage. Somebody should be thinking about that.

headlineQuote: If one buyer with AI does the work of three, then the other two deserve retraining on full pay.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old lead buyer** at Brightwell Medical Supply, stocking independent pharmacies on low pay.
She uses **AI tools daily** and built the alerts that run her mornings.
She has **under a month's savings**, a master's loan and few similar jobs nearby.
She'd lead the change and push for **shared gains**, while worrying about colleagues like Owen.
With time she plans a move into **pharmacy regulation** or quality; two years leaves her nothing to land on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even an early adopter would have nothing to land on.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income** for the gap and short free **courses** leading straight into new jobs.
